questions.question: Notice issued by government generally appears in
questions.answer:
**(A)** Newspapers

A government notice is meant for the public at large, and the medium that reaches the public is the **newspaper** (or the official gazette, published like one). A school or court notice board reaches only the people who pass it.

questions.question: What does the notice give to the readers?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Information

A notice conveys **information** — an announcement of an event, a loss, a change or a rule — to a well-defined group of readers. It does not greet them, and although it may invite them to a function, the invitation is the *content* of the information, not the purpose of the form.

questions.question: We should not include .................... in report writing.
questions.answer:
**(A)** Personal comment

A report is an objective record: it includes the **data collected** and the **information given by witnesses**, but not the reporter's **personal comments**, opinions or feelings. A comment turns a report into an article and destroys its credibility.

questions.question: Which one is a component of article writing?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Heading / Title

An article must have a **heading or title** (usually with the writer's name below it) and a series of paragraphs. Greetings and thanks belong to a speech; a salutation belongs to a letter.

questions.question: A formal letter starts with
questions.answer:
**(B)** Sender's address

A formal letter opens with the **sender's address** (with the date written below it), then the receiver's address, the subject line, the salutation and the body. The writer must be identified before the person addressed.

questions.question: What does the poet expect the fisherman to do?
options: Not to go in the sea
questions.answer:
**(A)** Not to harm the whales

In "Keeping Quiet" the poet imagines that in the moment of silence "Fishermen in the cold sea / would not harm whales". He does not ask them to give up the sea or to sit idle for ever — only to pause and see what their work does.

questions.question: What did Kamala Das say to her mother?
questions.answer:
**(D)** See you soon, Amma

At the airport the poet looks at her mother's "pale as a late winter's moon" face and says only, "**see you soon, amma**" — the poem's last line, and an attempt to hide her fear behind a cheerful word. It is repeated twice, as if saying it again would make it true.

questions.question: What blots the maps of the slum children?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Dirty slums

In "An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum" Spender says that for these children the map on the wall is a mockery and that "**their world**" is a slum: the poem's "map" is blotted by the **dirty slums** in which they live, not by the geography it shows. The "maps" of their lives are the "cramped holes" and the "slag heap" outside the window.

*(This chapter is outside the current syllabus but the question appears in this paper.)*

questions.question: Why was the roadside stand built?
options: So that people can wait here
To make it a bus stop
questions.answer:
**(C)** To earn money

The villagers built the stand to sell their produce to the passing cars and to "feel" some "city money in hand" — it is a small business, not a waiting shed or a bus stop. Its failure to earn that money is the poem's grievance.

questions.question: Franz looked for opportunities to skip school to do what?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Collect birds' eggs

Franz looked for opportunities to skip school "to look for birds' eggs" or "to go sliding on the saar" — the boy's pleasures that the school kept him from. It is exactly this carelessness that the last lesson makes him ashamed of.

questions.question: The ragpickers have no identity, but they have
questions.answer:
**(C)** Ration cards

In "Lost Spring" the ragpickers of Seemapuri live without an identity and without permits, but they hold **ration cards** that let them vote and buy grain — "food is more important for them than their identity".

questions.question: Mukesh belonged to a family of
questions.answer:
**(C)** Bangle makers

Mukesh's family are **bangle makers** of Firozabad: his father and grandfather worked at the glass furnaces, and his grandmother has not seen a full meal in her life. Mukesh, however, says he will be a motor mechanic — the first in the family to want something else.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: Which program was the author a part of?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Students on Ice Program

Tishani Doshi travelled to Antarctica as part of the "**Students on Ice**" programme, founded by the Canadian Geoff Green, which takes school and college students to the polar regions to give them a first-hand understanding of the earth's fragility.

questions.question: 'Why are we different from other Japanese?' Who said this?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Hana

**Hana** says this, in her own mind, as she and Sadao decide what to do with the wounded American: "Why are we different from other Japanese?" The question is the story's moral centre — the Sadaos are Japanese patriots who cannot hand a dying man back to the sea.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: What kind of atmosphere does Antarctica have?
questions.answer:
**(D)** All of these

Antarctica has the **coldest, driest and windiest** atmosphere on earth — the three records belong to the same continent. Tishani Doshi notes that it is "the coldest, driest, windiest continent", and that its ice holds most of the world's fresh water.

questions.question: The American soldier had been
questions.answer:
**(B)** Shot

The American prisoner of war had been **shot**: Dr. Sadao finds the bullet still lodged in him, "dangerously near the kidney", and has to cut it out. The wound is a gunshot wound, not a stab or a beating.

questions.question: Who was Charley's wife?
options: A woman at the third level
questions.answer:
**(D)** Louisa

Charley's wife is **Louisa**, who is worried about his "waking-dream wish to escape" and takes him to his psychiatrist friend Sam. Charley buys two tickets to Galesburg on the third level — one for himself and one for her.

questions.question: How old was the prince when he ridiculed the astrologer?
questions.answer:
**(A)** 10 days

The prince was **ten days old** when he spoke — an infant in the cradle — and asked the astrologer how anyone could know the manner of his death, since "all those who are born will one day have to die". The astrologer answered, "the death will come from the Tiger".

questions.question: What kind of a person is Roger's mother in Jo's opinion?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Wicked and stupid

Jo, listening to the story, thinks Roger's mother is **wicked and stupid** for taking her son back to the wizard and making him smell like a skunk again. She wants her father to make the wizard hit the mother; Jack refuses, and the quarrel between father and daughter is the real subject of the story.

*(This chapter is outside the current syllabus but the question appears in this paper.)*

questions.question: Which story did Mr. Lamb narrate to Derry?
questions.answer:
**(D)** The Beauty and the Beast

Mr. Lamb tells Derry the story of **Beauty and the Beast** — the tale in which a girl learns to love a beast because she looks past his appearance. It is exactly the lesson he wants Derry, whose face was burnt, to hear.

questions.question: What problem was faced by the Champaran Indigo sharecroppers?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Were forced to grow Indigo

The Champaran sharecroppers were **forced to grow indigo** on three-twentieths of their land and to surrender the harvest as rent to the British landlords. When synthetic indigo made the crop worthless, the landlords took money from the peasants to release them from the arrangement — and it is this injustice that Gandhi came to fight.

questions.question: Rajkumar Shukla was
questions.answer:
**(A)** A sharecropper

Rajkumar Shukla was a **poor sharecropper** from Champaran — "illiterate but resolute". He came to the Lucknow Congress session in December 1916 to complain about the injustice of the landlord system and would not let Gandhi go until he agreed to visit Champaran.

questions.question: Make-up room looked like a
questions.answer:
**(C)** Hair cutting salon

In "Poets and Pancakes" the make-up room at the Gemini Studios, with its "bright bulbs" and its mirrors and its smell of "Pancake" greasepaint, looked like a **hair-cutting salon** — a row of chairs, a crowd of actors and the "office boy" (the author) carrying the make-up around.

questions.question: The boy in the make-up room was jealous of whom?
options: Subbu's success and his closeness to the boss
questions.answer:
**(D)** Subbu's success and his closeness to the boss

The "boy" in the make-up room — the author, Kothamangalam Subbu's junior — is jealous of **Subbu's success and his closeness to the boss**. Subbu was the studio's most gifted man, the boss's favourite, and the chapter is the author's wry account of working beside him.

questions.question: Sophie's best friend was
questions.answer:
**(C)** Jansie

**Jansie** is Sophie's classmate and closest friend — the practical girl who warns her not to dream about boutiques and about Danny Casey, and who, in the end, is the one who spreads the story of Sophie's "meeting".

questions.question: What kind of girl is Sophie?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Day dreamer

Sophie is a **day dreamer**. She invents a meeting with the footballer Danny Casey, plans a boutique she has no money to open, and prefers her fantasies to the biscuit factory her friend Jansie accepts. The story's irony is that she half-believes her own invention.

questions.question: Bama was a/an
questions.answer:
**(B)** Tamil writer

Bama is a **Tamil Dalit writer** — the author of "We Too Are Human Beings", the second half of "Memories of Childhood", in which she recalls the day she learnt what untouchability meant.

questions.question: The lesson 'Memories of Childhood' is
questions.answer:
**(C)** An autobiography

"Memories of Childhood" is **autobiographical**: it prints two extracts from the autobiographies of two women — Zitkala-Sa's "The Cutting of My Long Hair" and Bama's "We Too Are Human Beings" — each recalling an episode of childhood humiliation that shaped the writer's later life.

questions.question: Who is the writer of the novel 'The Name of the Rose'?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Umberto Eco

*The Name of the Rose* is by the Italian novelist and semiotician **Umberto Eco**, who is one of the writers interviewed in Christopher Silvester's chapter "The Interview" and who explains there that he writes "in the cracks of time".

questions.question: Pancake was the brand name of the
questions.answer:
**(B)** Make-up material

**Pancake** was the brand name of the **make-up material** used at the Gemini Studios — a thick, greasy paste applied by the actors before shooting. The chapter opens with the author's memory of carrying those "Pancake" tins to the make-up room.

questions.question:
Read the passage on Dasrath Manjhi and answer any six of the following:
(a) What was done by Dasrath Manjhi?
(b) How did the hill act as a barrier?
(c) What inspired him to build a road?
(d) What picture do we get of Dasrath?
(e) How did he build the road?
(f) What lesson does he teach us?
(g) Give the synonyms of (i) keeping apart (ii) succeed in.
(h) Find the word from the passage which means 'invincible'.
questions.answer:
### (a)

**Answer.** Dasrath Manjhi, 31 years old, **set out to carve a 1 km long path through a rocky hillside**. He was "a man who built a road through the mountain", and he did it **by his own efforts, his drive and his indomitable determination**, using the simplest of tools — a chisel, rope and a hammer.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Dasrath Manjhi, 31 years old, set out to carve a 1 km long path through a rocky hillside."

**Why he did it.** He "wanted life to be easier for his fellow villagers", because the hill kept the villages in isolation and his wife had died for want of a hospital that he could not reach in time.

### (b)

**Answer.** The hill **kept the villages in isolation**. It was so slow and difficult to cross that the villagers **took hours just to reach the nearest market town**, and **children had to walk eight km to reach school**. In an emergency a patient could not reach a hospital at all.

**The passage's own words.**

> "The hill kept the villages in isolation. They took hours just to reach the nearest market town. Children had to walk eight km to reach school."

**What it cost him.** It was this barrier that killed Manjhi's wife: she died "since she could not reach the hospital on time".

### (c)

**Answer.** The **death of his beloved wife** inspired him: she "died since she could not reach the hospital on time" because the hill stood between the village and the town. His grief became the motive for the work, and his wish "to make life easier for his fellow villagers" kept him at it.

**The passage's own words.**

> "What empowered a single man to accomplish such an enormous task was his beloved wife, who died since she could not reach the hospital on time."

**The larger point.** Manjhi's road was not built for fame or reward — "not expecting rewards of any sort" — but so that no other family would lose a life for want of a path.

### (d)

**Answer.** We get the picture of a man of **extraordinary patience, courage and determination** — "his drive and his indomitable determination". He worked **alone**, with the **simplest tools — a chisel, rope and a hammer** — and **without expecting any reward**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "He did it by his own efforts, his drive and his indomitable determination. Not expecting rewards of any sort he did it using the simplest of tools — a chisel, rope and a hammer."

**Added colour.** He bore the **taunts and ridicule of his own villagers** ("though most villagers taunted and ridiculed him") and went on cutting the rock; the passage presents him as the model of patient, unglamorous heroism.

### (e)

**Answer.** He built it **by his own efforts, alone, with his own hands**, using only **a chisel, a rope and a hammer**, cutting a **one-kilometre path through the rocky hillside** bit by bit over years, without machines, money or help — and without expecting any reward.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Not expecting rewards of any sort he did it using the simplest of tools — a chisel, rope and a hammer."

**What makes it remarkable.** The task would normally need a team and explosives; Manjhi had neither. The phrase "indomitable determination" is the passage's explanation of how a single man finished what a contractor would have called impossible.

### (f)

**Answer.** He teaches us that **patience is the greatest virtue that leads to success** — and, with it, determination and selfless service.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Though most villagers taunted and ridiculed him, Dasrath taught us that patience is the greatest virtue that leads to success."

**The lesson in full.** A single man with a chisel can move a mountain if he keeps at it; and the motive matters — Manjhi worked not for reward but so that others might live more easily. The ridicule of the villagers, which he ignored, is part of the lesson too.

### (g)

**Answer.** (a) Keeping apart — **isolation**; (b) Succeed in — **accomplish**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "The hill kept the villages in **isolation**."

> "What empowered a single man to **accomplish** such an enormous task..."

**Note.** Both words are the passage's own; give one word each, and do not paraphrase ("being separate", "do well in") when the paper asks for the synonym from the passage.

### (h)

**Answer.** **Indomitable** — as in "his drive and his **indomitable** determination".

**Why.** "Invincible" means unconquerable, impossible to defeat; "indomitable" means exactly that — a spirit that cannot be subdued. The passage uses it of the determination with which Manjhi cut his road through the rock.

questions.question: Is Saheb happy working at the tea stall? Explain. (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **No, Saheb is not really happy at the tea stall**, though he earns there. He gets **eight hundred rupees and all his meals**, and he no longer has to scrounge in the garbage dumps — but the work has taken away the one thing he valued, his freedom.

**Why.** As a ragpicker Saheb was his own master: he walked where he liked, with his plastic bag on his shoulder, and the garbage was "wrapped in wonder" because a coin might be hidden in it. At the tea stall he is **somebody's servant**: he must stand behind the counter, fetch and carry, and wait for the owner's orders from morning to night. Anees Jung notes that the author is less happy about the job than Saheb himself, precisely because "the steel cannedister" that he carries now is not his.

**In one line.** He has exchanged a hard freedom for a small security, and the chapter's pity is that a child of his age should have to make that exchange at all.

questions.question: Who was Rajkumar Shukla? Why did he come to Lucknow? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Rajkumar Shukla was a **poor sharecropper from Champaran**, in Bihar — "illiterate but resolute". He was one of the peasants bound by the British landlords' arrangement to grow indigo on part of their land and surrender the harvest as rent.

**Why he came to Lucknow.** He came to the **December 1916 annual convention of the Indian National Congress** at Lucknow **to complain about the injustice of the landlord system in Bihar** and to ask the leaders for help. Somebody advised him to meet Gandhiji, and he approached him there.

**What followed.** Gandhi told him he had appointments in Cawnpore and elsewhere, but Shukla followed him from place to place for weeks — to Cawnpore, to Calcutta, to Patna — until Gandhi could not avoid him. That persistence took Gandhi to Champaran and began the first civil-disobedience movement in India.

questions.question: Where is the poetess going and what does she think of the mother? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poetess is **driving from her parents' home to Cochin**, to catch a plane — she is leaving her mother behind and going away to her own work and city.

**What she thinks of her mother.** Sitting beside her in the car, she sees the old woman **dozing, "open mouthed", her face "ashen like that of a corpse"**, and she realises "with pain that she was as old as she looked". The mother's face is "pale as a late winter's moon", and the sight brings back "that old familiar ache" — her childhood fear of losing her mother, and behind it the fear of age and death.

**How she hides it.** She looks out at "young trees sprinting" and "merry children spilling out of their homes" to escape the thought, and at the airport she smiles and says, "see you soon, amma" — a cheerful line that conceals her fear.

questions.question: Why did the Maharaja want to marry and to whom? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The Maharaja wanted to marry **to complete his tally of a hundred tigers**. He had killed **seventy tigers** in his own kingdom of Pratibandapuram in ten years, and tigers there had become extinct — so the astrologer's prophecy could not be fulfilled unless he found more tigers elsewhere.

**To whom.** He chose **a princess of a state which had a large tiger population**. His "master strategy" was to marry into such a state so that he could visit his father-in-law's kingdom and kill **five or six tigers on every visit**. He married the princess whose photograph showed such a state, and in this way killed **ninety-nine tigers** in all.

**The irony.** The hunt for the hundredth tiger, which he never found in the forest, was satisfied by a **wooden toy** — and that toy killed him.

questions.question: How did Sadao finally help the white man to escape? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** When the American was fully recovered, Dr. Sadao decided to **send him to the unguarded island in the sea** rather than hand him over to the police.

**What he gave him.** He gave him **his own boat, clothes, food, bottled water and his flashlight**, and told him to row to a **little deserted island nearby** and wait there until he saw a **Korean fishing boat** pass — many of them passed that way. If the food ran out before a boat came, he was to signal with **two flashes of the flashlight**; he was not to signal in darkness, because he could be seen.

**The escape.** The young American came down into the darkness of the garden, took the boat and went. Sadao waited for the signal, and when there was **no flash of light by sunset** he knew that the prisoner had gone from the island — "safe and well". He felt "relieved, rewarded and happy".

questions.question: Who is Edla? What are her thoughts about the peddler? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Edla Willmansson is the **daughter of the ironmaster** at the Ramsjö ironworks. She is young, kind and unmarried, and she is the only person in the story who treats the peddler as a human being from the first.

**Her thoughts about the peddler.** When her father brings the ragged stranger home, thinking him an old regimental comrade, Edla sees at once that he is a **poor peddler and probably a thief** — she notices his fright and his "hungry" look. She does not turn him out. She says that he shall stay and eat with them on Christmas Eve, and she tells him that he must not be afraid.

**What she does.** She gives him a Christmas gift, lends him her father's clothes and speaks for him when the others suspect him. Her one condition — that he return the money he has taken — is what finally turns the peddler into an honest man.

questions.question: Who is Mr. Malkani? What help does he do to Gandhiji? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Mr. Malkani was a **school teacher at Motihari**, the capital of Champaran — a government servant who taught in the local high school.

**How he helped Gandhiji.** When Gandhi arrived in Motihari to gather evidence about the peasants' grievances, **Malkani gave him shelter in his own house and helped him organise the enquiry**. He collected the sharecroppers' statements, introduced Gandhi to the local workers and stood by him when the police began to take notice. It was Malkani who was with Gandhi when the news came that a peasant had been maltreated in a nearby village.

**The price he paid.** As a government school teacher he was taking a real risk, since the district officials were hostile; the chapter's point is that the Champaran movement was built by such local men — Malkani, Kripalani and the lawyers — as much as by Gandhi himself.

questions.question: What kind of students were studying in the elementary school classroom? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The children of Spender's slum classroom are **starved, neglected and diseased**. They sit "like rootless weeds", their hair "torn round their pallor", and one of them is "a paper-seeming boy with rat's eyes". A tall girl sits with her head "weighed down", and another boy has "squirrel's eyes" and looks at the teacher with fear.

**What is wrong with them.** They are thin and weak from hunger, their faces pale and lifeless, and their bodies marked by disease and neglect. They are the children of the slum — of "slag heap" and "cramped holes" — and their whole world is a narrow street of fog and "endless night".

**The poem's charge.** Spender says that for such children the map on the wall and the portrait of Shakespeare are a mockery: they are "far from the gusty waves" of life, and the schoolroom offers them a world they cannot reach.

*(The chapter is outside the current syllabus but the question appears in this paper.)*

questions.question: You are Niti/Mohit, a student of Class 12, S. N. +2 College, Ranchi. You have lost your I Card in the college campus. Write a notice for the school on the notice board. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**S. N. +2 COLLEGE, RANCHI**

**NOTICE**

*18 September 2024*

**LOST I-CARD**

I have lost my **College Identity Card** somewhere in the college campus. I am Niti of Class XII, Section B, Roll No. 24, and the card must have slipped out of my folder on **Monday, 16 September**, most probably in the corridor outside the chemistry laboratory or in the canteen.

**Identifying details.** The card is a **blue laminated card** with my photograph on the left and the college seal partly scratched at the top right corner. It carries the number **SNC/2024/1247**.

The loss is a serious inconvenience, since the card is required at the gate, in the library and at the examination hall. Anyone who finds it is requested to hand it over to me in Class XII-B or to deposit it at the college office, and to inform the office clerk. A small reward will be given for the trouble.

**Niti**
Class XII-B
Roll No. 24

**Format points.** Name of the institution, the word NOTICE, the date, **what was lost, when and where, identifying marks and what to do**, and the signature with the class — the whole within 50 words in a normal notice; the 250-word limit allows the details above to be spelled out, but do not pad it beyond identification and request.

questions.question: You are Kavita/Karan, the cultural secretary of +2 College, Dhanbad. Write a suitable notice for your school notice board requesting the names of students to participate in the Annual Function to be organised in your school. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**R. S. +2 COLLEGE, DHANBAD — CULTURAL COMMITTEE**

**NOTICE**

*12 November 2024*

**ANNUAL FUNCTION — ENTRIES INVITED**

The **Annual Function** of the college will be held on **Saturday, 14 December 2024, at 4 p.m. in the college auditorium**. Students who wish to take part in the cultural programme should give their names to the undersigned through their class representatives **on or before 25 November 2024**.

**Items.** (1) Group dance — folk and classical; (2) solo song — Hindi and regional; (3) one-act play and skit; (4) elocution on "My India of 2047"; (5) poetry recitation; (6) instrumental music; (7) fashion show on "Handloom of Jharkhand".

**Conditions.** Each participant may offer a maximum of two items; the selection committee will audition the entries on **28 and 29 November in the auditorium at 2 p.m.**; music tracks must be submitted on a pen drive at the time of the audition; costumes and props are the participants' responsibility, though the college will meet the cost of the stage and the sound system. A rehearsal for the selected items will be held on 12 December.

The list of selected items will be displayed on the notice board on 2 December.

**Karan**
Cultural Secretary

**Format points.** The institution, the word NOTICE, the date, the event with **date, time and venue**, the items, the **entry deadline**, the audition dates and conditions, and the signature with the designation.

questions.question: Write a letter to the Editor of a newspaper complaining about the frequent voltage fluctuation and low-voltage power supply in your area. You are Reema/Manoj, Road No. 139, Raj Nagar, Ranchi. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Road No. 139**
**Raj Nagar, Ranchi**
**18 July 2024**

The Editor
*The Hindustan Times*
Ranchi

**Subject: Frequent voltage fluctuation and low-voltage power supply in Raj Nagar**

Sir

Through the columns of your esteemed daily I wish to draw the attention of the electricity department to the **frequent voltage fluctuation and low-voltage supply** in Raj Nagar.

For the last two months the supply in our locality has been so poor that the fans barely turn in the afternoon, and the voltage dips every evening between seven and ten — exactly the hours when children study and the family sits together. There have been four prolonged cuts this month apart from the daily "fluctuation", and each dip is accompanied by a flicker that has already damaged the refrigerators and the inverter of our neighbours.

**The damage is real.** Low voltage burns out motors and compressors; a sudden surge destroyed two television sets on our street last week. Students preparing for examinations cannot read, and the elderly in the colony suffer in the summer heat. Repeated complaints to the sub-divisional office have brought no inspection.

I request the department to **check the transformer and the load on the feeder**, to replace the old cables in the lane, and to publish a maintenance schedule so that the residents can plan.

Yours faithfully
**Manoj**

**Format points.** Sender's address and date, addressee, subject line, the problem with **specific instances and consequences**, and a numbered or linked set of remedies — within 250 words.

questions.question: Write a report about a road accident involving a car and a bus. Give the details of the people injured. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**THREE INJURED AS BUS OVERTURNS AFTER HITTING CAR**

*By a Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 20 February 2024.** Three persons were injured, one of them seriously, when a speeding private bus hit a car and overturned on the Ranchi–Ramgarh highway near the Ormanjhi turn this morning.

According to the police, the bus, carrying about forty passengers from Ramgarh to Ranchi, tried to overtake a truck and struck the car coming from the opposite direction at about 8.30 a.m. The bus then swerved, hit the road divider and turned over on its side. The car, a white hatchback, was thrown off the road and its front portion was completely crushed.

**The injured.** The car's driver, **Ramesh Kumar, 34, of Ormanjhi**, has been admitted to the RIMS trauma centre with head injuries and a fractured arm and is said to be serious. Two passengers of the bus — **Savitri Devi, 52**, and a boy of about ten, **Aman** — were treated at the Sadar hospital for cuts and bruises and discharged. No other passenger was seriously hurt, since most of them were thrown clear as the bus slowed before overturning; the conductor, however, received injuries to his shoulder and is in hospital.

The bus driver fled from the spot, leaving the vehicle behind. A case of rash and negligent driving has been registered at the Ormanjhi police station, and the police are looking for him. Local people complain that the stretch has no speed-breakers and no patrol, and that this is the third accident at the turn in two months.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, the **sequence of the accident**, the numbers and names of the injured with the nature of their injuries and the hospital, the action taken, and the local grievance — within 250 words.

questions.question: Write an article on the effects of mobile phone in students' life. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**THE MOBILE PHONE IN A STUDENT'S LIFE**

The mobile phone is the most useful and the most dangerous thing a student carries. In one small screen it gives a library, a classroom, a dictionary and a telephone; it also gives a thousand interruptions a day.

**What it gives.** A student can watch a lecture by the best teacher in the country, look up a word in a second, keep in touch with parents while travelling, and call for help in an emergency. During the pandemic the phone and the laptop were the school. For a first-generation learner in a small town, this is a genuine revolution.

**What it takes.** The same phone shortens attention, breaks sleep and eats the hours that should go to play and to books. A student who studies with a phone beside him is not studying: the notification arrives, the game waits, and the page is read three times without being understood. The blue light at midnight makes the morning dull, and the constant scrolling makes the quiet thinking that study requires almost impossible. Then there is the harm that is harder to see: the comparison with other people's lives, the bullying in group chats, the photographs that are never really deleted.

**What should be done.** Not prohibition, which never works, but discipline: no phone during study hours, no phone in the bedroom at night, and a rule that the phone is a tool and not a companion. The device is neutral; the habit is what decides whether it builds a student or wastes him.

**Format points.** A title, a balanced treatment of **both** sides, a paragraph on remedies, and a firm conclusion — within 250 words.

questions.question: You are Mukul/Mansi of Bal Krishna +2 High School, Ranchi. A Corona Vaccination camp was organised in your school for the 15 to 18 years age group. Write a letter to your friend explaining your unfamiliar experience. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Bal Krishna +2 High School**
**Ranchi**
**18 March 2024**

My dear Rohan

I must tell you about something completely new that happened at school last week — a **Corona vaccination camp** for students between fifteen and eighteen, and I was in the first group.

The whole school was turned into something like a hospital. The assembly hall had been divided into three rows of tables with boards reading "Registration", "Screening" and "Observation", and there were doctors from the district hospital in white coats and two nurses with a trolley of small vials. I had never seen our hall so quiet. A volunteer gave me a form, a doctor asked me whether I had fever or had been ill recently, and then I was asked to sit on a chair and roll up my left sleeve.

The injection itself was nothing — a small pinch, and then a strange cold spreading in my arm. The difficult part was the waiting. For half an hour we sat in the "Observation" row, and nobody spoke much; a boy next to me kept asking whether his arm was supposed to feel heavy. I was given a certificate with the date and the name of the vaccine, and a boiled sweet, which I thought was a nice touch.

My arm ached for two days, and I felt a little feverish on the first night. But I keep thinking of the morning: an entire school, hundreds of us, sitting quietly in rows while a needle went from arm to arm. I had only read about such things.

Do write and tell me when your school holds its camp.

Your loving friend
**Mansi**

**Format points.** Address and date, familiar salutation and close, **the unfamiliar details the question asks for** — the arrangements, the injection, the waiting, the certificate — and a personal reflection, within 250 words.
